This is the absolute LAST post I ever expected to be making on the Monday of my bodybuilding show week.

After months of weighing every gram of food, tracking every calorie, hitting my workouts, doing my cardio, practicing my posing, and preparing myself mentally, physically, and spiritually to step on stage this Saturday, I spent this past weekend binge eating in a way I’ve never experienced before.

And when I say binge eating, I don’t mean I went out and enjoyed a cheat meal or ate a little more than I was supposed to.

I mean I completely lost control.

I kept eating long after my stomach was telling me to stop. I was physically uncomfortable, I wasn’t even enjoying the food anymore, and yet I continued eating.

And the scariest part wasn’t even the amount of food I consumed.

It was what was going through my head while I was doing it.

At a certain point, it felt like I was intentionally sabotaging myself. Like there was a part of me that wanted to ruin everything I had worked so hard for.

And I’ve spent the last couple of days asking myself WHY.

Was I afraid I wasn’t going to look good enough on stage? Was I afraid of disappointing myself? Was I putting so much pressure on myself that I subconsciously wanted a way out?

I don’t have all the answers.

But those are some uncomfortable questions I’ve had to start asking myself.

After the first binge, I told my coach Chris Elkins everything. Every single thing I ate. We talked about it, and the plan was to move forward, reassess, and take things day by day.

The next day, I got right back to my routine. Tracked my food, followed my plan, and genuinely thought I had moved past what happened.

Then nighttime came.

What started as one extra bite of food turned into another binge. And this one was even worse than the first.

I can’t even explain how disappointed I felt afterward.

Not because I had eaten food that wasn’t on my plan. But because I had reached a point where I felt like I couldn’t stop myself from doing something I knew was hurting me.

I woke up physically miserable. My face was extremely swollen, my body felt awful, and I was looking at myself in the mirror trying to understand how I had gotten here.

And now here I am.

Five days away from the competition I’ve spent months preparing for, roughly 10 pounds heavier than I was going into the weekend, and genuinely uncertain whether I’m going to step on stage this Saturday.

Chris believes competing is still an option. Part of me wants to finish what I started. Another part of me wonders whether postponing until November would be the better decision.

Because I know how much work I put into this prep. And I also know that the choices I made this weekend have consequences.

I’m not going to sit here and blame anybody else. I’m not going to pretend it didn’t happen. And I’m definitely not going to ask anyone to feel sorry for me.

But I also don’t want to spend the rest of my life beating myself up over two days.

I made those choices. I have to own them. And now I have to figure out how to move forward.

One thing this weekend has forced me to recognize is just how much pressure I’ve been putting on myself. Not only with bodybuilding, but with life in general.

Constantly working. Constantly thinking about what’s next. Constantly being on my phone. Constantly feeling like I need to be doing MORE.

And somewhere along the way, I stopped giving myself enough room to just live.

So regardless of whether I compete Saturday or in November, some things are going to change.

I’m prioritizing my sleep. I’m taking real breaks from social media. I’m giving myself time to recover. And I’m going to take a serious look at my relationship with food and the pressure I’ve been putting on myself.

I’m not going to pretend I’ve figured everything out in 48 hours. I haven’t.

And I don’t want to turn this into some inspirational story about how I fell down and immediately got back up stronger than ever.

I’m still figuring it out.

posts.text:
For those of you in the English speaking community who don't know, a Salvadoran streamer named Komanche was confirmed dead yesterday.

He had recently been accused of sexual assault, an allegation he denied publicly. Friends and fans didnt care to listen, and turned their backs on him.

Now the accuser has deleted tweets, and many are now seeing the truth for what it was.

I met him at TwitchCon and liked him alot. We hung out that weekend and I saw who he was, a guy that just wants everyone to laugh.

When the world turns on you before you've had a chance to answer, you start wondering whether anything you say will ever change how people see you.

You can explain yourself and still be left wondering whether anyone actually heard you, or whether they've already decided what kind of person you are.

Allegations like these follow you into every part of your life. You can be walking down the street and catch someone looking at you, and immediately wonder whether they're thinking:

“rapist”

“monster”

You hide yourself from the world, become ashamed of not just who you are but the person you're going to become, because you feel there's been a death wish casted on you and every moment of your life will bare it.

Then you go home, and it follows you there too, and in your sleep, you have nightmares of people abandoning you, leaving you. And as you wonder what you did to deserve this, and need a shoulder to cry on, those who will still answer you will tell you "just move on".

I haven't had a second in the past year where I haven't wondered whether my parents and family still love me the same way, or whether they think of me differently now. This goes not just for them, but anyone who i've ever been friends with. I'm ashamed to message friends Merry Christmas or even wish them a happy birthday.

I know that fear doesn't tell me what they actually believe. But having to wonder that about people who have known you your entire life is something I don't know how to explain.

And having false allegations broadcasted live to millions as other creators feed off it, and go with the narrative before even bothering to hear yours makes it impossible to get away from.

Your entire career, everything you worked for, starts to feel like a distant dream. Achievements that just yesterday were the proudest moments of your life become things you're almost embarrassed to look back at. You look at old pictures of yourself being happy and remember what it felt like to be proud of who you were, without wondering what everyone else thought.

Your past becomes something you want to run away from, but when you try to picture your future, you're afraid it will feel just as bad. You want to move on, but you don't know where you can go that this won't follow.

I worry about my false allegations following me into a family I haven't even had yet.

What if I have a son someday, and someone recognizes me at his soccer game? What if their opinion of me becomes the reason they won't let their kids play with my son?

What if the woman I marry has friends who have already decided who I am before they've ever met me? Does she spend her life having to explain why she's with me?

These are things I think about when I try to picture my future. I worry about people I love having to answer for what strangers believe about me.

Someone living with that much isolation can become so overwhelmed that death starts to feel like the only escape. That's how hard it can become to see that a future is still possible.

That's why I stand by calling for criminal accountability when someone is proven to have fabricated allegations and their actions amount to a crime.

Anyone making an accusation that serious has a responsibility to understand what is at stake. The sympathy the accuser receives in a day and attention cannot justify decades of damage to another person's life.

The attention moving on doesn't mean the person accused gets their life back.

I wish he'd called. I wish I could've been there for him. And I wish I'd known.

RIP Komanche.
